excerpt: StreamSets is a low-code platform for building streaming data pipelines. Software AG bought it in 2022 and IBM acquired it in July 2024; it is now IBM StreamSets.
content:
StreamSets makes software for building data pipelines: the plumbing that moves data continuously from sources such as databases, applications, logs and message queues into data warehouses, data lakes and analytics tools. Its pitch has always been that pipelines can be designed visually, with a drag-and-drop canvas, and that they cope with data drift, meaning changes in the structure of incoming data that would break hand-written code. Today it is sold as IBM StreamSets.

IBM's product page describes a low-code interface for designing and deploying streaming pipelines, prebuilt processors that detect and adapt to data drift, support for structured, semi-structured and unstructured data, and a Python SDK. It can run as a software-as-a-service on AWS, Azure or Google Cloud, in a customer's own cloud account or virtual private cloud, or on the customer's own servers. IBM lists use cases such as fraud detection, customer 360 views, operational event processing and streaming data for AI, and it now sits inside IBM's watsonx.data integration family.

StreamSets has changed hands twice. In March 2022 RTInsights reported that Software AG had agreed to buy the company for €524 million (about $582 million), giving the German software firm entry into cloud data integration; Girish Pancha was StreamSets' CEO at the time. On 1 July 2024 IBM completed its purchase of StreamSets and webMethods from Software AG. IBM's press release said it would offer StreamSets as a premium feature in watsonx.data alongside DataStage and Databand, and that the two products together served more than 1,500 companies. IBM's quarterly filing with the US Securities and Exchange Commission puts the price for both at about $2.3 billion in cash.

IBM does not publish StreamSets prices on its product page. It offers a free trial and asks buyers to contact sales.

This page is research, not a review. We have not tested StreamSets; facts come from IBM's pages, an SEC filing and the reporting under Sources.

profile.platform: SaaS on AWS, Azure or Google Cloud; self-managed or on-premises
profile.starts_at: Free trial; pricing from IBM sales
profile.summary_short: Low-code streaming data pipelines, now part of IBM watsonx.data integration

team.name: Girish Pancha
team.role: CEO of StreamSets at the 2022 Software AG acquisition

use_cases: Streaming database changes into a cloud data warehouse such as Snowflake or Databricks
Building pipelines with a visual canvas instead of hand-written code
Handling schema changes (data drift) without broken pipelines
Feeding real-time data to fraud detection and customer 360 systems
Moving data across hybrid and multi-cloud environments

fit: data engineering teams in large enterprises, especially existing IBM customers
companies running hybrid or on-premises data infrastructure
teams that want visual pipeline design with a Python SDK for automation
not_fit: small teams wanting transparent self-serve pricing
projects that only need simple batch copies between two SaaS tools

pricing.intro: IBM does not list StreamSets prices on its product page. It offers a free trial and directs buyers to sales for a quote.

pros: Visual pipeline design with drift handling
Runs in IBM's cloud SaaS, your own cloud or on-premises
Backed by IBM's support and integration with DataStage and watsonx.data
cons: Two ownership changes since 2022 may concern some buyers

alternatives.intro: Other data integration and streaming pipeline tools.

items.name: Fivetran
items.what: Managed connectors that load data into warehouses
items.difference: Fully managed ELT with usage-based pricing.

items.name: Confluent
items.what: Data streaming platform built on Apache Kafka
items.difference: Event streaming backbone rather than a visual pipeline designer.
